Eleven of fourteen biomarkers are strongly right-skewed, so we analyse them on a log scale

Reading it

Black line: median. Red line: the clinical threshold.

Log axes are labelled in the original units, so a value can be read straight off.

Transform: log for 11 skewed markers, then z-score; 0.3% of values beyond ±4 SD are clipped. Histograms show the central 99.6%.

The biomarkers travel in families: sugar, lipids and insulin, liver, inflammation, kidney

Reading it

Rows and columns are ordered by similarity, so families appear as warm blocks along the diagonal.

The strongest pair is glucose–HbA1c (ρ .63); HDL runs against triglycerides (−.50).

Spearman ρ on the raw values · average-linkage ordering on 1 − |ρ| · diverging scale, white = 0.

Projected onto its main axes, the data is one cloud, not islands

What it means

Any clustering of this data cuts a continuum into regions. Mean-shift finds one density peak holding 95% of people.

So the question becomes: do the regions mean anything the blood did not already say?

PCA on the 14 standardised biomarkers · Gaussian KDE contours · mean-shift bandwidth from the 20% quantile of distances.

Part 2 of 5
Cluster

Cut the cloud into regions — and test whether the cut survives.

k-means with 100 restarts, a second and third method that fail differently, bootstrap stability, and one step either side of the chosen k.

UMAP layout, for display only: it keeps neighbourhoods, not distances, so the gaps between colours are not measurements.

k = 4 is the most detailed partition that still survives resampling

Reading it

Silhouette is low everywhere (0.11 at k = 4): consistent with a continuum, and unable to choose.

Bootstrap stability is: 0.89 at k = 4, 0.77 at k = 5.

k-means, 100 restarts, seed 42 · 30 bootstrap re-fits scored by adjusted Rand index · Gaussian mixture (diagonal) and Ward linkage as methods that fail differently.

One step either side: at k = 3 two phenotypes merge, at k = 5 an older renal group splits off

Reading it

Each band is a group of people; its colour is the k = 4 cluster they belong to.

At k = 5, the new grey group is older (median 71) with high creatinine and urine albumin, drawn from all four clusters.

Same transform and seed at k = 3, 4, 5 · flows are exact counts.

Validate

Do the groups differ on 22 things the algorithm never saw?

The test that can fail: diagnoses, blood pressure, self-rated health and money, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction and an effect size beside every q-value.

The 454 adults whose blood meets the diabetes criteria: told never told

Built from blood alone, the clusters still differ on 21 of the 22 things they never saw

Reading it

Right and high: large and certain. The grey band marks differences under 0.2 SD — too small to matter whatever the q.

Colour = the cluster that departs most. Income is real but small; diagnosis is large.

Kruskal–Wallis (continuous), χ² (binary) · Benjamini–Hochberg across 22 tests · n = 1,986–2,290 per test.

What this establishes — and what it does not

Established

  • Four stable regions in the biomarker space (bootstrap ARI 0.89), each persisting at k ± 1.
  • They differ on 21 of 22 variables they never saw, with large effects on diagnosis, BMI, sex and age.
  • 31% of lab-defined diabetes is undiagnosed (31% weighted), concentrated outside the Dysglycaemic cluster.
  • A consistent signature: held-out recovery 0.98 against a 0.25 baseline.

Not established

  • That the phenotypes are natural groups: the data is one continuum (one density mode, silhouette 0.11).
  • Anything over time: NHANES is cross-sectional, with no follow-up outcome in our data.
  • Causation: income, sex and BMI are associations, and several act through each other.
  • US prevalence of the clusters: clustering is unweighted; diagnoses are self-reported.

The seven questions every cluster analysis must answer, answered

1Which variables built the clusters, which describe them?14 biomarkers built them; 22 external variables describe them. No overlap.
2How many clusters, chosen how, and what happens at k ± 1?k = 4 by bootstrap stability (ARI 0.89 vs 0.77 at k = 5). k = 3 merges Inflammatory and Hepatic; k = 5 splits an older renal group.
3How many tests, which correction for which family?22 omnibus tests, Benjamini–Hochberg across variables; pairwise Mann–Whitney / Fisher with Holm within each variable.
4An effect size beside every p-value?Kruskal–Wallis ε², Cramér’s V, standardised differences, odds ratios per SD.
5Cluster sizes on every figure?810 · 581 · 660 · 239.
6Can a model recover the labels on held-out patients?Balanced accuracy 0.98 (L1 logistic), 0.92 (random forest); baseline 0.25.
7What do the clusters predict that the clustering never saw?Diagnoses, blood pressure, self-rated health, sex and income: external-only model 0.53 vs 0.25.

Three things the blood knew

Four regions, not four islands — and they differ on 21 of 22 things the clustering never saw.

A third of lab-defined diabetes is undiagnosed, and most of it looks like its neighbours, not like diabetes.

Money matters, modestly: the income gradient is real, small, and travels through weight and sex.
